content_list.content_text: André Breton, the founder of Surrealism, saw cinema as a way of liberating the subconscious. As his collaborator Philippe Soupault wrote: "We believed that cinema would present extraordinary possibilities for expressing, transfiguring and realizing dreams."

In 1924, Breton wrote the Surrealist Manifesto and, that same year, filmmaker René Clair (1898-1981) directed Entr'acte (1924), a blend of slapstick comedy and dream logic. Made to be shown during the intermission of Francis Picabia's ballet Relâche, then playing at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris, the film features cameos by Picabia and the artists Man Ray (1890-1976) and Marcel Duchamp (1887-1968).

content_list.title: The Surrealist Manifesto
content_list.description:
Published in 1924 by André Breton, the Surrealist Manifesto brought the world a new way of looking at art.

Following Dadaism (a movement that advocated opposition to any kind of balance), Surrealism imposed so-called psychic automatism, "in its pure state, by which one proposes to express - verbally, by means of the written word, or in any other manner - the actual functioning of thought; dictated by thought, in the absence of any control exercised by reason, exempt from any aesthetic or moral concern."

According to Breton, he and the writer Soupault gave the name Surrealism to the new mode of expression they had at their disposal, in homage to Guillaume Apollinaire.

In this manifesto, the Surrealist principles are declared, such as freedom from logic and the embrace of a higher reality, called the "marvelous."

content_list.content_text: Picabia conceived the film together with Clair and intended it as an attack on Breton, yet Entr'acte is considered a Surrealist film. It opens with a superimposition of images and relies on skillful editing to create surprising effects: a ballerina turns into a bearded man and a hearse travels along the tracks of a roller coaster.

information.contentText: Clair used superimpositions of various images in Entr'acte, such as this one, of a ballerina filmed from below to create an unsettling effect.

content_list.content_text: Although director Germaine Dulac (1882-1942) was never part of the movement, she too was interested in the unconscious and used Antonin Artaud's Surrealist screenplay for La coquille et le clergyman (The Seashell and the Clergyman, 1928), a fragmented, lyrical narrative centered on the erotic hallucinations of a clergyman. However, Artaud felt that Dulac's fluid camerawork and optical effects were incompatible with Surrealism, and he staged a loud protest with other artists at the film's premiere.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from The Seashell and the Clergyman (1928)
information.contentText: The provocative images of Dulac's The Seashell and the Clergyman blend in fantasy to explore the subconscious.

content_list.content_text: The Seashell and the Clergyman was overshadowed by the hugely acclaimed Un chien andalou (1929), directed by Luis Buñuel (1900-1983), who also wrote the screenplay together with Salvador Dalí. The film helped the two of them become accepted as Surrealists, and Buñuel's second film, L'Âge d'Or (1930), was also faithful to the movement.

The film caused a scandal and there was a riot at its premiere, after which it was banned for almost 50 years. Buñuel broke with the Surrealists in 1932 but continued to make films in that vein throughout his career. Although he later went into exile from his native Spain, in 1960 he accepted an invitation from Francisco Franco's government to make a film.

quote.quote: Surrealism is based on the belief in the superior reality of certain forms of previously neglected associations, in the omnipotence of dream (...).
quote.author: André Breton

content_list.content_text: The director showed he had lost none of his subversive verve, and the film Viridiana (1961) - with its parody of Leonardo da Vinci's painting The Last Supper, featuring a band of rowdy beggars in place of the apostles - was banned in the country until Franco's death.

Surrealism gradually made its way into commercial cinema. In 1945, Dalí was hired to create a dream sequence for Alfred Hitchcock's (1899 -1980) Freudian thriller Spellbound (1945). The following year, he collaborated with Walt Disney (1901-1966) on an animated short, Destino (2003), which was shelved until 2003, when it was finally completed by the studio's animators.

The influence of Surrealist cinema is significant, and its dreamlike imagery, non sequiturs, use of Freudian symbolism and bizarre superimpositions are present in the films of directors such as Federico Fellini (1920-1993), Kenneth Anger (1927) and David Lynch (1946).
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Dominic Power, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

content_list.content_text: In the summer of 1929, a Parisian audience gathered for the screening of a new film. Backstage, the director waited with a bucket full of stones to throw at the spectators in case the picture was poorly received.
content_list.content_title: A Landmark for the Movement That Inspired It

information.contentText: On a moonlit balcony, a man (Buñuel) sharpens his razor. He then holds the head of a young woman (Simone Mareuil) and uses the blade to slice her eyeball, sending the vitreous humor running down her face. Buñuel said he used the eye of a dead calf for the scene.

content_list.content_text: On screen, a razor is honed on a leather strop. A man with a cigarette dangling from his mouth tests the blade on his thumb, drawing blood. A young woman stares at an invisible audience, expressionless. The man's hand parts her eyelids. A full Moon hangs in the sky and a pointed cloud passes across it. The razor slices the eyeball.

In his autobiography, Luis Buñuel describes how he and the artist Salvador Dalí worked on Un Chien Andalou: "Our only rule was very simple: no idea or image that might lend itself to a rational explanation of any kind would be accepted. We had to open all doors to the irrational and keep only those images that surprised us, without trying to explain why." The film offers the illusion of a narrative: it begins with the simplest of all invocations of a story, "Once upon a time... ", and this intertitle imposes an arbitrary and meaningless chronology.

quote.quote: Surrealism is destructive, but it destroys only what it considers to be shackles limiting our vision.
quote.author: Salvador Dalí

content_list.content_text: The film is a stream of subversive images: a man in partial drag, wearing a bonnet and a short skirt over a suit, rides a bicycle through the streets of Paris; an enigmatic young woman pokes at a severed hand lying in the street; ants crawl out of a hole in the palm of a living person's hand; to reach the object of his desire, a man has to pull harnesses tied to two priests and two grand pianos, each with a dead donkey on top. Un Chien Andalou may not have been the first Surrealist film, but it is a landmark for the movement that inspired it.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Dominic Power, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.title: Un Chien Andalou
movies.overview: Un Chien Andalou is a classic European avant-garde surrealist film from the cooperation of director Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dali. The film changed the way people made movies.

movies.title: The Seashell and the Clergyman
movies.overview: Obsessed with a general's woman, a clergyman has strange visions of death and lust, struggling against his own eroticism.

movies.title: Entr'acte
movies.overview: Premiered as an intermission for the Swedish ballet production Relâche at the theater of Champs Elysées in Paris.

movies.title: Ballet mécanique
movies.overview: Ballet Mécanique (1923-4) is a Dadaist post-Cubist art film conceived, written, and co-directed by the artist Fernand Léger in collaboration with the filmmaker Dudley Murphy (with cinematographic input from Man Ray). It has a musical score by the American composer George Antheil. However, the film premiered in silent version on 24 September 1924 at the Internationale Ausstellung neuer Theatertechnik (International Exposition for New Theater Technique) in Vienna presented by Frederick Kiesler. It is considered one of the masterpieces of early experimental filmmaking.

movies.title: The Starfish
movies.overview: Two people stand on a road, out of focus. Seen distorted through a glass, they retire upstairs to a bedroom where she undresses. He says, "Adieu." Images: the beautiful girl, a starfish in a jar, city scenes, newspapers, tugboats. More images: starfish, the girl. "How beautiful she is." Repeatedly. He advances up the stair, knife in hand, starfish on the step. Three people stand on a road, out of focus. "How beautiful she was." "How beautiful she is." "Beautiful."

movies.title: The Blood of a Poet
movies.overview: Told in four episodes, an unnamed artist is transported through a mirror into another dimension, where he travels through various bizarre scenarios. This film is the first part of Cocteau's Orphic Trilogy, which consists of The Blood of a Poet (1930), Orpheus (1950) and Testament of Orpheus (1960).
